title: 第七章尸变第八章 画壁第九章云萝公主
lines: 第七章尸变
阳信县蔡家庄，有位蔡姓里正，村里人都称他蔡老头。蔡老头在村口开了家客店，专接待南来北往的行商走贩。店面不大，统共不过四五间客房，却日日收拾得窗明几净，房钱也收得公道，过往客商赶路歇脚，都偏爱往他这儿来。
这年秋日，蔡老头家中刚遭了丧事，新寡的儿媳撒手人寰。儿媳嫁入蔡家三年，性子勤快又温顺，里里外外的家务打理得妥妥当当，是村里少有的好媳妇。怎料一场风寒来势汹汹，年纪轻轻二十一岁，便匆匆去了，咽气时双眼都未能合上。蔡老头老两口心疼不已，可人死不能复生，只得暂且将儿媳的棺木停放在后院东头的空房里，等着挑个吉日再下葬。
那间停棺的空屋，紧挨着客店最东端，墙外头便是车马通行的大路，夜里总能听见外头的风声与脚步声，本就透着几分清冷。
这天傍晚，客店来了四位客商。四人赶着几匹驮满布匹的骡子，一路风尘仆仆，皆是二十出头的壮实后生，说话爽朗，嗓门敞亮，一进门便喊着腹中饥饿，想寻个住处歇息。
蔡老头连忙迎上前，搓着双手满脸歉意：“几位客官对不住，今日往来客人多，店里只剩东头那一间空房了。只是那屋子……不大干净，实在委屈的话，几位不妨在堂屋打个地铺凑合一晚？”
领头的客商姓杨，为人爽快，压根没把“不干净”放在心上，摆了摆手道：“出门在外哪有那么多讲究，我们赶了一天路，累得快散架了，有个能躺的地方就行。老爷子，只管备饭便是！”
蔡老头张了张嘴，想把屋里停棺的事说出口，话到嘴边又咽了回去。他知晓赶路之人的辛苦，也怕直说出来吓着众人，只得吩咐老伴炒了几样小菜，烫了一壶热酒，伺候四人吃饱喝足。四人打着哈欠，跟着蔡老头往东边那间空屋走去。
蔡老头站在院子里，看着那屋的灯火亮起，又渐渐熄灭，望着紧闭的房门长长叹了口气，终究还是转身回了屋。他终究没敢告知四人，这屋里停着的，是自己刚过世不久的儿媳。
四个客商进了屋，点灯细看，屋内靠墙摆着一张床铺，被褥铺得齐整，倒也还算洁净。床对面立着一扇门，门上垂着布帘，帘后黑漆漆一片，看不清里头光景。
杨老大将随身包袱往床头一丢，开口道：“我先歇了，你们三个挤一挤。”说罢脱鞋上床，倒头便睡，其余三人也累到了极致，挨着彼此躺下，不多时便鼾声四起，屋子瞬间陷入沉寂。
半夜时分，杨老大被尿意憋醒，迷迷糊糊坐起身，刚要下床，忽然听见对面布帘后传来“窸窸窣窣”的声响，像是有人在缓慢挪动，又像是衣物摩擦的轻响，在寂静的夜里格外刺耳。
他猛地清醒几分，揉了揉眼睛，借着窗外透进来的淡淡月光，朝帘后望去。
帘后正是那口停尸的棺材，棺盖竟不知何时被挪开了一道缝，一道身影缓缓从棺中坐起。
杨老大浑身汗毛瞬间倒竖，头皮发麻，想张嘴呼喊，喉咙却像被堵住一般发不出半点声音；想起身逃跑，双腿软得像煮透的面条，半点力气都使不上，只能僵在原地，眼睁睁看着那道身影从棺材里爬出来。
月光洒在那人脸上，是个年轻女子，身着一身素白丧服，面色惨白如纸，双目紧闭，嘴唇泛着青紫色，直挺挺立在棺前，一动不动，似在侧耳听着床上的动静。
杨老大屏住呼吸，连大气都不敢喘，心脏狂跳得快要撞碎胸膛。
女子静立片刻，忽然朝着床边缓缓移动。她走路的模样极为怪异，并非抬脚迈步，而是双脚离地，轻飘飘地往前飘，像一片被风推着的白纸，悄无声息地靠近床铺。
她飘到床前，低下头，对着床上熟睡的三个客商，俯下身，一个接一个地对着他们的面颊轻轻吹气。
杨老大吓得魂飞魄散，却依旧不敢动弹分毫。他眼睁睁看着三个同伴被吹气后，脸色以肉眼可见的速度变得惨白，呼吸渐渐微弱，身体慢慢僵硬，转眼便成了三具直挺挺的木俑，再无半点声息。
女子吹完三人，缓缓直起身，转过身，轻飘飘地朝着杨老大的方向飘了过来。
不知哪来的一股力气，杨老大猛地掀开被子，连滚带爬地滚下床，踉跄着扑到门口，双手哆嗦着拔开门闩，一把推开房门，一头扎进了屋外漆黑的夜色里，拼了命地狂奔。
身后没有脚步声，只有一阵“呼呼”的风声，紧紧跟在他身后，像是那女子追了上来。
杨老大不敢回头，只顾着埋头往前跑，脚下生风，恨不能多长两条腿。
他穿过院子，跑过堂屋，直奔客店大门，见大门紧锁，也顾不上开锁，手脚并用地翻过院墙，纵身跳了出去。墙外是一条宽敞大路，路两旁是黑漆漆的庄稼地，夜里风一吹，庄稼叶沙沙作响，更显阴森。他辨不清方向，只知道朝着前方死命跑，远离那间恐怖的屋子。
content_en:
Chapter 7 Corpse Transformation
In Caijiazhuang, Yangxin County, there was a man named Cai Lizheng, and everyone in the village called him Old Man Cai. Old Man Cai opened an inn at the entrance of the village, specializing in receiving merchants traveling from north to south. The store is not big, with only four or five guest rooms in total, but the windows are kept clean every day, and the rent is paid fairly. Passing merchants who are on their way to rest often prefer to come here.
In the autumn of this year, Old Man Cai's family had just suffered a funeral, and his newly widowed daughter-in-law passed away. The daughter-in-law has been married to the Cai family for three years. She is diligent and docile, and takes care of the housework inside and outside. She is a rare good daughter-in-law in the village. Unexpectedly, a cold wind came fiercely, and at the young age of 21, he left in a hurry, unable to close his eyes when he died. Mr. Cai and his wife were heartbroken, but there was no resurrection, so they had to temporarily put their daughter-in-law's coffin in an empty room at the east end of the backyard, waiting to pick an auspicious day for burial.
The empty room where the coffin is kept is located next to the eastern end of the inn. Outside the wall is the main road for carriages and horses. You can always hear the sound of wind and footsteps outside at night, and it is a bit cold.
That evening, four merchants came to the inn. Four people drove several mules laden with cloth, and they were all stout young men in their early twenties. They spoke cheerfully and had bright voices. As soon as they entered the door, they complained that they were hungry and wanted to find a place to rest.
Old Man Cai hurriedly came forward, rubbing his hands and apologizing: "I'm sorry, the guests. There are so many customers today, and there is only one empty room at the east end of the store. But the room... is not very clean. If you are really aggrieved, why don't you guys make a bunkhouse in the main room for one night?"
The leading merchant's surname was Yang. He was a cheerful person and didn't take "dirtyness" to heart at all. He waved his hand and said: "There's no need to be so particular about going out. We've been traveling all day and are so tired that we're almost falling apart. All we need is a place to lie down. Master, just prepare food!"
Old Man Cai opened his mouth and wanted to tell him about the coffin in the room, but he swallowed the words again. He knew how hard it was for people on the road, but he was afraid of frightening everyone by saying so, so he ordered his wife to cook a few side dishes, boil a pot of hot wine, and wait for the four of them to eat and drink. The four of them yawned and followed Old Man Cai towards the empty room to the east.
Old Man Cai stood in the yard, watching the lights in the house turn on and then gradually go out. He looked at the closed door and sighed, and finally turned around and went back to the house. After all, he did not dare to tell the four of them that the person parked in this room was his daughter-in-law who had just passed away.
The four merchants entered the house, lit the lamp and took a closer look. There was a bed against the wall in the house. The bedding was spread neatly, but it was still clean. There was a door opposite the bed, and a curtain hung on the door. It was so dark behind the curtain that it was difficult to see what was going on inside.
Mr. Yang threw his baggage on the bedside and said, "I'm going to rest first. You three can squeeze in together." After that, he took off his shoes and went to bed, then fell asleep. The other three were extremely tired and lay down next to each other. Soon they started snoring, and the room instantly fell into silence.
In the middle of the night, Mr. Yang woke up due to the urge to urinate. He sat up in a daze and was about to get out of bed when he suddenly heard a "rustling" sound coming from behind the curtain on the opposite side. It seemed like someone was moving slowly, or like the sound of clothing rubbing against each other. It was particularly harsh in the quiet night.
He woke up suddenly, rubbed his eyes, and looked behind the curtain with the faint moonlight coming through the window.
Behind the curtain was the coffin for the corpse. Unexpectedly, the lid of the coffin was moved open a crack, and a figure slowly sat up from the coffin.
The hair all over Yang's body suddenly stood up, his scalp was numb, he wanted to open his mouth to shout, but his throat seemed to be blocked and he couldn't make any sound. When he wanted to get up and run away, his legs were as soft as boiled noodles, and he couldn't use any strength. He could only freeze in place, watching the figure climb out of the coffin.
The moonlight shines on the man's face. He is a young woman, dressed in plain white mourning clothes. Her face is as pale as paper, her eyes are closed, and her lips are purple. She stands upright in front of the coffin, motionless, as if she is listening to the movement on the bed.
Boss Yang held his breath, not even daring to take a breath. His heart was beating so fast that it was about to break his chest.
The woman stood quietly for a moment, then suddenly moved slowly towards the bed. The way she walked was extremely weird. Instead of taking steps, her feet lifted off the ground and floated forward lightly, like a piece of white paper pushed by the wind, quietly approaching the bed.
She floated to the bed, lowered her head, leaned over the three merchants sleeping on the bed, and blew gently on their cheeks one by one.
Boss Yang was so frightened that he still didn't dare to move at all. He watched helplessly as his three companions were blown away, their faces turning pale at a speed visible to the naked eye, their breathing gradually becoming weaker, their bodies slowly stiffening, and in the blink of an eye they turned into three upright wooden figurines, making no sound at all.
After the woman finished blowing to the three of them, she slowly straightened up, turned around, and floated lightly in the direction of Boss Yang.
With a burst of strength from nowhere, Mr. Yang suddenly opened the quilt, rolled out of bed, stumbled to the door, unlatched the door with trembling hands, pushed the door open, and plunged into the dark night outside, running as fast as he could.
There were no footsteps behind him, only a "whooshing" sound of wind, following closely behind him, as if the woman was catching up.
Boss Yang didn't dare to look back, he just kept running forward with his head down, the wind blowing under his feet, wishing he could have two more legs.
He crossed the courtyard, ran through the main room, and went straight to the door of the inn. Seeing that the door was locked, he didn't bother to unlock it. He climbed over the courtyard wall with his hands and feet and jumped out. Outside the wall is a broad road with dark crop fields on both sides. When the wind blows at night, the crop leaves rustle, making it even more eerie. He couldn't tell the direction, so he only knew to run forward, away from the scary room.
